articles.title: Winners named in Jersey charity's first animal photo contest
articles.summary: The JSPCA encouraged islanders to take the photos as part of its first photography competition.
articles.body:
The winners of a local animal charity's first photography competition have been announced.

The JSPCA said its first Favourite Animal Moments Photo Competition invited people aged five and upwards to submit photos "celebrating the special bond between animals and people".

The charity said winning photographs would feature in its 2027 calendar with all proceeds supporting animal welfare services across the island.

Chief executive of the JSPCA Pam Aubert said the charity was "over the moon with the response" to its first launch of the competition.

She said: "Jersey is home to so many talented photographers and, of course, amazing animals and the entries we received really proved this.

"We plan for this competition to become something islanders look forward to every year as we celebrate the animals that enrich all of our lives."

Adam Heath, was part of the judging panel, and said judges were impressed by the quality of entrants.

He said: "I have to say that we found judging really difficult, due to the huge response and the extraordinary variety of images submitted.

"We tried to choose photos people will enjoy looking at and hope it generates much needed funds to support the fantastic work of the JSPCA for the people and pets of Jersey."

Tina won the title of Little Paws Photographer (ages five to eight), Eliza was Young Animal Photographer (ages nine to 12), Nathan was Teem Photographer (ages 13 to 17) and the Adult Photgrapher/ Overall Winner (age 18+) was Hannah Saxby.

The JSPCA said photographs were judged on "creativity, composition and their ability to tell a story" and added age appropriate judging criteria was in place for younger entrants.

articles.title: Aos 96 anos, eleitora de Mossoró vai às urnas e já pensa na próxima  | G1
articles.standfirst: Geisa Fernandes completa 97 anos em outubro, já foi mesária e conta que fica ansiosa para votar antes mesmo do dia da eleição.
articles.summary: Aos 96 anos, Geisa Fernandes foi às urnas neste domingo (4), em Mossoró. Ela contou que fica ansiosa para votar antes mesmo do dia da eleição.
articles.body:
Aos 96 anos, Geisa Fernandes mantém o hábito de participar das eleições. Moradora de Mossoró durante toda a vida, ela não abriu mão de votar e foi às urnas neste domingo (4) no Colégio Diocesano Santa Luzia, no bairro Santo Antônio.

🔎 No Brasil, o voto é obrigatório para pessoas alfabetizadas entre 18 e 70 anos. A partir dos 70 anos, o voto passa a ser facultativo.

Dona Geisa completa 97 anos no próximo dia 24 de outubro. Mesmo sem ter mais a obrigatoriedade de votar por causa da idade, ela faz questão de participar do processo eleitoral e diz que fica ansiosa para a chegada do dia da votação.

“Eu quero dar o meu voto, eu gosto de votar. Quero participar”, contou.

A relação de Geisa com as eleições é antiga. Ela contou que já atuou como mesária em eleições anteriores.

Neste domingo, Geisa chegou ao local por volta das 8h. Depois de votar, permaneceu sentada em um banco enquanto aguardava o filho. Ela contou que o processo foi rápido. “Estou feliz porque eu votei como eu queria”, disse.

A expectativa de Geisa com as eleições não termina quando o voto é depositado. Segundo ela, quando uma eleição acaba, já começa a ficar ansiosa pela próxima. “Daqui a quatro anos, venho de novo votar.”

Em Mossoró, Geisa Fernandes, que completa 97 anos no dia 24 de outubro, foi às urnas neste domingo (4) para votar — Foto: Antonio Linoelson/Inter TV

articles.title: Atriz brasileira Renata Mietto é presa pelo ICE em aeroporto | G1
articles.standfirst: Renata Alves Mietto, de 26 anos, foi detida pelas autoridades dos EUA quando se preparava para embarcar para o Havaí para comemorar o aniversário da mãe.
articles.summary: A atriz brasileira Renata Alves Mietto foi detida pelo ICE no aeroporto de Los Angeles e segue presa há um mês devido a problemas em seu status migratório.
articles.body:
A atriz brasileira Renata Alves Mietto — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

O que deveria ser uma viagem em família para comemorar o aniversário da mãe terminou em uma prisão que mudou completamente a vida da atriz brasileira Renata Alves Mietto, de 26 anos.

Ela foi detida no aeroporto de Los Angeles no dia 27 de agosto, quando se preparava para embarcar para o Havaí.

Segundo Márcia Rilda Alves dos Reis, a filha passou normalmente pela segurança e pelo raio-x, entrou com o passaporte e, quando já estava no portão de embarque, foi abordada e presa por agentes do ICE que estavam à paisana.

“Nós achávamos que, nessa questão de pegar voo, eles só estavam pegando quem tivesse algum tipo de crime. Mas a gente não sabia que eles estavam prendendo qualquer pessoa. Quando você passa na segurança, eles têm essa ligação direta com o ICE, essa impressão que a gente tem", contou Márcia.

Renata chegou aos Estados Unidos em 2016, aos 16 anos.

No país, ela concluiu o ensino médio e estudou Artes Cênicas na Utah Valley University. Há pouco mais de três anos, vive em Los Angeles, onde também construiu sua carreira profissional.

Como atriz, participou de produções como The Cool Kids e, paralelamente, tornou-se proprietária de uma empresa de limpeza que hoje emprega mais de 20 pessoas. Segundo a mãe da jovem, Márcia, o grande sonho de Renata é ser atriz de cinema.

A mãe explica que a filha perdeu o status de permanência nos Estados Unidos há cerca de dois anos, após receber uma orientação jurídica equivocada.

Transferida algemada da Califórnia para o Texas

Após ser presa no aeroporto, Renata foi inicialmente levada para um centro de detenção em Los Angeles e, posteriormente, transferida para Adelanto, na Califórnia, onde permaneceu por mais de 20 dias.

Enquanto isso, sua família tentava acompanhar o processo à distância com advogados para encontrar uma forma de tirá-la da prisão.

No dia 18 de setembro, Renata participou de uma audiência.

A defesa pediu que ela pudesse responder ao processo em liberdade, mas o pedido foi negado sob o argumento de que ela representaria um risco. Segundo a mãe, Renata nunca cometeu nenhum crime e estaria detida exclusivamente por estar sem status migratório regular.

Para Márcia, a situação é difícil de compreender e ainda mais difícil de suportar.

“Para mim, como mãe, é um desespero tão grande ver a minha filha passar por isso. Porque ela não cometeu nenhum crime. Ela não tem motivo algum para estar presa só pelo fato de estar sem status. Isso não significa que eles podem fazer essa covardia, e não é só com ela, mas com tantas outras pessoas ali dentro. Ali tem mães, pessoas que estão presas sem motivo. Eles estão pegando todo mundo e fazendo essa covardia. Eu quero tirar minha filha dali, urgente”, conta Márcia aos prantos.

No dia seguinte à audiência, 19 de setembro, a situação ficou ainda mais angustiante para a família.

Renata foi transferida para El Paso, no Texas. A transferência, segundo o relato da mãe, foi marcada por horas de espera e restrições físicas.

“Eu sei que ela ficou muito tempo, ficou horas dentro de uma van sem poder fazer xixi, sem poder tomar água, algemada nos pés, na cintura, nas mãos, sentada por horas até entrar no voo. Chegando lá, ficou das 21h até o dia seguinte às 17h sentada, quando ela foi colocada em um quarto”, relata a mãe reforçando que a todo o momento a filha permaneceu algemada.

“Durante todas essas horas, a noite inteira, com frio. Ela pediu para poder usar o suéter dela que estava na mala. Mas sumiram com a bolsa de mão dela, com os documentos, com o cartão de crédito, com joias. Até hoje, a mala não apareceu”, conta.

Segundo Márcia, Renata também teria apresentado inchaço nas pernas e nos pés e dor de garganta depois de passar tantas horas sentada em um banco pequeno e em um ambiente gelado.

A família tenta agora autorização para visitá-la, mas, até o momento, não conseguiu agendar com o centro de detenção. Do lado de fora da prisão, familiares e advogados tentam encontrar uma saída para o caso.

“Ela queria pelo menos voltar na casa dela”

Segundo Márcia, a filha está seguindo o aconselhamento jurídico e solicita a saída voluntária do país. Mesmo sendo contra a vontade da filha, a mãe acredita que essa seria a solução.

“Ela queria pelo menos voltar na casa dela, pegar as coisas dela. Ela tem um coelho que já tem seis anos. É tanta coisa, sabe? Emocionalmente. É tanto sentimento de injustiça. Apesar de ela ter ficado esse tempo fora de status, não é ilegal, é fora de status. Ela é uma menina que entrou aqui com 16 anos, estudou aqui. Eu pagava todos os estudos dela. Paguei muito caro para ela estudar. Então, ela fez faculdade. E, infelizmente, a gente teve uma orientação errada de um advogado. Ela está emocionalmente devastada, descontrolada”, descreve Márcia.

Segundo a advogada de imigração e também advogada do Consulado de Los Angeles, Gisele Ambrósio, desde junho aumentou muito o número de detenções nos aeroportos, inclusive em embarques nacionais, como aconteceu com a Renata.

“Existe uma gama variada de pessoas que estão sendo presas pelo ICE. Por exemplo, pessoas fora de status, com asilo pendente, com pedidos de extensão de visto, pedidos até de green card pendentes, pessoas com ordem de deportação final e até com permissão de trabalho, mas sem aprovação final do caso”, relata Gisele.

A advogada destaca a queda na procura por novos pedidos de green card, cidadania e vistos de residência nesse momento marcado pelo endurecimento das políticas migratórias nos Estados Unidos.

Dados do governo americano revelam uma queda de 45% no número de pedidos de imigração recebidos pelo USCIS no segundo trimestre de 2026, em comparação com o mesmo período de 2025. E a advogada faz um alerta:

“Eu acho que qualquer imigrante, nesse momento, que tiver um caso pendente com a imigração, não deve viajar antes de consultar seu advogado de imigração. Tenha sempre o número do seu advogado escrito em algum lugar ou de cor. Deixe cópias da sua documentação com seus amigos. Tenha sempre um plano do que fazer se algo acontecer com você, se você tiver filhos, tiver bens. É muito importante já deixar esse planejamento todo feito, caso algo aconteça com você nos Estados Unidos nesse momento”, aconselha a advogada.

articles.title: Kalil (PDT) vota em Belo Horizonte | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato ao governo de MG votou neste domingo (4) na Escola Estadual Governador Milton Campos, no bairro Lourdes.
articles.summary: Candidato ao governo de MG votou neste domingo (4) na Escola Estadual Governador Milton Campos, no bairro Lourdes.
articles.body:
Alexandre Kalil, candidato do PDT ao governo de Minas, chega ao local de votação neste domingo (4), em Belo Horizonte. — Foto: Ernane Fiuza - TV Globo

O candidato ao governo de Minas Gerais, Alexandre Kalil (PDT) votou neste domingo (4) na Escola Estadual Governador Milton Campos, no bairro Lourdes, em Belo Horizonte. Ele chegou ao local de votação por volta de 10h, acompanhado de familiares.

Antes de votar, Kalil falou sobre a campanha e ressaltou que está confiante para um possível segundo turno.

"Foi uma campanha muito organizada e a sensação que tenho é de dever cumprido. To muito orgulhoso de ter nome e numero para concorrer a um cargo tão importante. Além disso, estou muito confiante para um segundo turno", falou o candidato.

O local de votação do candidato apresentava muita movimentação. Kalil é um dos eleitores que tiveram seções alteradas. Ele votava na unidade 1 do colégio e teve que vir pra unidade 2 e ficou por volta de 40 minutos na fila.

articles.summary: Veja onde e como votaram os candidatos do Espírito Santo neste domingo (4).
articles.body:
Candidatos ao governo do Espírito Santo votam neste domingo; veja — Foto: g1

Os candidatos ao governo do Espírito Santo votaram neste domingo (4) em cidades da Grande Vitória. Veja abaixo, em ordem alfabética, como foi a votação de cada umob.

Breno Barcelos (Missão), candidato ao Governo do Espírito Santo, vota em Vitória — Foto: Guilherme Marques

Breno Barcelos (Missão), candidato ao Governo do Espírito Santo, votou às 9h deste domingo (4) no Colégio Darwin, no bairro Jardim da Penha, em Vitória.

“Tivemos uma adesão muito grande da população, muita gente cooperando com a campanha [...] foi uma campanha que não tinha dinheiro, mesmo assim tivemos um trabalho multiplicado por pessoas que entenderam nosso projeto, que começou no Espírito Santo com o pé direito”, disse.

Helder Salomão votou em Cariacica — Foto: Analu Fagundes/Rede Gazeta

Helder Salomão (PT), candidato ao Governo do Espírito Santo, votou neste domingo (4) em Cariacica. Ele chegou ao local de votação por volta das 10h, acompanhado de sua equipe e de Célia Tavares (PT), candidata a deputada estadual. Helder votou às 11h.

“A nossa expectativa é que tenhamos um dia de democracia, o dia em que o povo vai escolher o futuro do Espírito Santo. Nós estamos confiantes. Há ainda mais de 50% de indecisos, isso mostra que a eleição está aberta", disse.

Rafael Demuner (UP), candidato ao Governo do Espírito Santo, vota em Vitória — Foto: Analu Fagundes

Rafael Demuner (UP), candidato ao Governo do Espírito Santo, votou às 9h deste domingo (4) no Colégio Salesiano, em Jardim Camburi, em Vitória. O candidato ao governo do Espírito Santo, acompanhado do assessor.

“Nós, da Unidade Popular conseguimos uma ótima candidatura e apresentamos nosso programa ao povo capixaba. A gente quer conquistar o governo do estado para tirar o poder da velha classe política e trazer para a classe trabalhadora", disse.

Ricardo Ferraço (MDB) vota em Vitória acompanhado da esposa, Vivian Coser — Foto: Jaciele Simoura

Ricardo Ferraço (MDB) votou às 8h30 na Escola da Ilha, na Praia do Canto, em Vitória. O atual governador chegou acompanhado da esposa, Vivian Coser, e do candidato ao Senado e ex-governador Renato Casagrande.

“Foram quase 50 dias de um diálogo intenso com a população capixaba, e meu otimismo e confiança vêm do reconhecimento que as pessoas têm pela transformação real que estamos fazendo no Espírito Santo”, disse.

articles.title: Eleições em Praia Grande: Avó de 80 e neto de 17 votam juntos | G1
articles.standfirst: Lea Maria de Jesus Carvalho, de 80 anos, fez questão de ir às urnas em Praia Grande. Já o neto Lucas Melo Carvalho, de 17, participou da eleição pela primeira vez.
articles.summary: Nas eleições em Praia Grande, Lea Maria, de 80 anos, e seu neto Lucas, de 17, exerceram a cidadania juntos para garantir um futuro melhor ao país.
articles.body:
Três gerações da família Carvalho votaram neste domingo (4), em Praia Grande (SP) — Foto: Jennyfer Lima/A Tribuna Jornal

Três gerações da família Carvalho se encontraram neste domingo (4), em Praia Grande , no litoral de São Paulo, em torno do mesmo compromisso: votar. De um lado, a aposentada Lea Maria de Jesus Carvalho, de 80 anos, que fez questão de ir às urnas mesmo sem ser obrigada; do outro, o neto Lucas Melo Carvalho, de 17, que votou pela primeira vez.

A família votou no Colégio Objetivo, na Vila Tupi, por volta das 11h. Enquanto aguardava a esposa para acompanhar a sogra até a escola onde ela votaria, o enfermeiro André Luis Melo Carvalho, de 54 anos, falou sobre as expectativas para o futuro do país.

“Eu espero que nosso País saia dessa recessão. Eu voto pelo voto de todos, que possamos sair da desigualdade”, afirmou. André também disse esperar que o próximo presidente governe para a população.

Moradora da Vila Tupi, Lea também fez questão de participar da eleição, apesar de o voto não ser obrigatório para ela. Segundo a família, a aposentada já votou outras vezes no mesmo local e não encontrou dificuldades de acessibilidade.

“Eu quero votar para lutar pelo meu neto”, disse Lea.

A fala da avó ganhou um significado especial para Lucas, que decidiu participar da eleição pela primeira vez. Segundo ele, a iniciativa partiu do próprio interesse em conhecer as propostas dos candidatos. “Eu vi a proposta dos candidatos e decidi votar pelo meu futuro”, contou.

Aos 17 anos, Lucas também disse esperar que o resultado contribua para o futuro do país. “Eu espero que ganhe o melhor para o futuro do Brasil.”

A escolha do neto também emocionou a família. Lucas disse considerar especial a disposição da avó em continuar participando das eleições aos 80 anos. “É bem fofo, eu acho bonito ela (a avó) querer votar para poder melhorar o meu futuro”, afirmou.

articles.summary: Candidata ao governo de MT votou neste domingo (4) na Escola Municipal de Ensino Básico Professora Alzira Valladares.

articles.body:
Se a ideia para a virada do ano é trocar a correria pela tranquilidade de um resort, o Atibaia Residence Hotel & Resort já prepara condições especiais para o Réveillon 2027. O pacote contempla o período de 29 de dezembro a 3 de janeiro, com mínimo de quatro noites, e foi pensado para famílias que querem celebrar o Ano Novo com diversão, gastronomia e momentos de descanso.

A proposta é reunir, em um mesmo lugar, atividades para crianças e adultos, permitindo que a família aproveite a viagem sem precisar montar uma programação diferente para cada dia.

A programação especial inclui uma Festa da Virada, com contagem regressiva, show ao vivo, recreação temática e atividades para diferentes idades.

A proposta do resort é transformar a chegada de 2027 em uma experiência que vá além da tradicional contagem regressiva, com atrações ao longo da hospedagem.

Para as crianças, a programação de recreação é organizada de acordo com as faixas etárias, com atividades acompanhadas por equipe especializada.

A noite da virada também conta com uma ceia especial, preparada especialmente para a ocasião. O pacote prevê um menu especial, gastronomia de alto padrão, música ao vivo e um ambiente pensado para reunir as famílias durante a celebração.

A ideia é que os hóspedes possam aproveitar a noite sem precisar sair do resort para organizar a ceia ou procurar um restaurante.

Outro destaque do pacote é o sistema All Inclusive. Durante a estadia, os hóspedes têm acesso a uma variedade de opções gastronômicas, além de drinks selecionados, petiscos, sobremesas e picolés, de acordo com as condições do pacote.

Com o sistema, a proposta é facilitar a experiência da família durante a viagem, concentrando alimentação e momentos de lazer dentro do próprio resort.

O resort também conta com três piscinas totalmente aquecidas, permitindo que os hóspedes aproveitem a estrutura mesmo quando as temperaturas estiverem mais baixas ou o tempo mudar.

Para as famílias que viajam com crianças, as piscinas fazem parte das opções de lazer disponíveis durante a estadia.

Por ser um dos períodos mais procurados do calendário, o Pacote de Réveillon possui vagas limitadas. Para quem pretende passar a virada em Atibaia e quer organizar a viagem com antecedência, a recomendação é consultar as condições do pacote e verificar a disponibilidade para o período desejado.

articles.title: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
articles.summary: Footage shows a drone hitting the Pivnichyi (Northern) Bridge as vehicles move across it, creating a large fireball.
articles.body:
Major bridges in Kyiv have been hit by Russian drone strikes for four consecutive days, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital.

Two people were injured when the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was struck on Sunday morning for the second day in a row, while the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times earlier in the week.

The latest attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to Kyiv in a show of support against Russia's continuing full-scale invasion.

Russia's military said it would be intensifying strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions. It earlier said it had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops.

Video footage of Sunday's strike, verified by the BBC, shows cars moving on Pivnichnyi Bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge.

Other videos and pictures have emerged on social media showing a gaping hole in the middle of a traffic lane on the bridge.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit.

Kyiv's eight bridges across the wide Dnipro River link the western (right) and eastern (left) parts, and many of the capital's estimated three million residents rely heavily on the metro lines and trains to travel across the city.

Some 500,000 vehicles use the bridges every day.

The two struck bridges are still standing - but the damage and restrictions to traffic and public transport have caused gridlock in parts of the capital at times.

"To get from the left bank to the right one and back - it's just hell," Kyiv resident Roman told the BBC on Sunday.

Large numbers of commuters cross the river, especially on weekdays. Repair teams are working to fix the damage and officials say they are planning temporary pontoon bridges, ferry services and even a tunnel under the river to keep Kyiv connected.

Klitschko also said a separate Russian drone strike had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy said on Sunday morning Russian drones had also attacked a warehouse in the north-eastern region of Sumy, killing one person.

Meanwhile, in the central city of Dnipro, six people were injured after a communications facility was struck, he said.

Ukraine's Air Force said that overnight Russia had launched 135 drones, including 52 jet-powered ones. It said that 125 projectiles had been shot down.

As emergency services responded to the incidents, Germany's Merz met Zelenksy in Kyiv. They laid wreaths to Ukrainian soldiers who have been killed in the war.

Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, writing on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.

"Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well."

Zelensky later said that a new aid package worth more than €1.3bn (£1.1bn; $1.5bn) had been agreed with Germany.

"These are weapons that will help [us] right now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter," he said.

As Merz was visiting Ukraine's Academy of Sciences building badly damaged in a Russian drone attack earlier this week, fresh air alert sirens were heard across the city. Two people were killed in that drone attack.

Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine.

He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us."

Zelensky said there would be "important agreements" made between Ukraine and Germany.

The Ukrainian president has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered Russian drones and also ballistic missiles.

The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier this week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had earlier said his military was carrying out retaliatory attacks following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities, despite the fact that it was the Kremlin that had first launched such attacks.

Putin began a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

The Russian foreign ministry on Saturday repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.

Responding to the warning, EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!"

German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying".

Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.

Klitschko warned that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.

Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable.

articles.title: Glastonbury Festival 2027 tickets sell out in 42 minutes
articles.summary: Thousands of people joined the queue in the hope of securing tickets to Worthy Farm.
articles.body:
Tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027 sold out in 42 minutes, organisers have said.

Thousands of people joined the online queue at 09:00 BST in the hope of securing tickets to the festival at Worthy Farm in Somerset, which returns from 23 to 27 June after a fallow year .

Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from the last event in 2025.

Headliners have yet to be announced but organiser Emily Eavis previously said the team was "very excited" and things were "coming together really well".

Glastonbury posted on Instagram shortly after 09:40 to announce that tickets had sold out, and notified those who were in the queue.

"Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply," the post said.

"There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in Spring 2027."

The first round of tickets, which were for coach packages, went up for sale on Thursday and sold out in less than half an hour.

Despite the increase in cost, Zoe Scott, who has been to the festival twice, said "the price is totally worth it".

"You're getting to see thousands of acts, there's over 100 stages," she said.

"It's such a vibe at Glastonbury- everyone's so happy and free-spirited. You're just on a constant high from friends, music and the sun is usually shining".

A couple who first met at Glastonbury will also be heading to Worthy Farm next year to celebrate their 20th wedding anniversary.

Nick and Helen Nugget from Amersham met through mutual friends at the festival in 2007 and will be returning next year with the same group.

Nick told BBC Your Voice that they were "absolutely delighted" to be going back.

The couple last went to the festival in 2011- although they were successful in securing tickets in 2019, they were unable to attend due to the adoption of their daughter.

Dave in London was in several groups all trying to get tickets through their laptops and phones on Sunday morning, and was successful.

He said: "Actually it seems like it's fairer this year than it's ever been.

"All the hacks that people used to use don't seem to have the same impact, and about a quarter of the people on the groups we are on managed to get tickets."

Sarah in Dorset was surprised she also managed to get hold of some.

She said: "A mobile phone on 5G in Shaftesbury seemed to be the optimal way to get tickets. We didn't even know Shaftesbury had 5G until this morning."

Among those who were not successful were Mat Chapman and his daughter Amy.

Mat told the BBC that he used to watch the festival on TV with Amy when she was little, promising to take her when she was five years old as "she always wanted to have her own flag that you could see on the telly".

Mat had hoped that after 20 years of trying, he would be able to beat the queue this year, on Amy's 26th birthday. Unfortunately he only ever moved from "two bar hell to three bar purgatory".

"There's always next year. We'll fly the flag there one day."

This year's Glastonbury tickets have breached the £400 mark for the first time.

Tickets have increased over the years, from £185 in 2010 to £408 for the upcoming 2027 line-up.

Most price rises have come since the pandemic, with tickets climbing from £318 in 2019 to a peak of £408 in 2027.

But unlike recent years, much of the 2010s saw relatively steady price hikes.

Any tickets from today's sale that are not paid for in full by the early April 2027 deadline will be put back into an official resale pool, festival organisers said.

The exact date for this is yet to be announced, but in previous years it has been in late April.

articles.title: Gay bar raid in Taiwan sparks protest; 51 detained under 'public morality' law
articles.summary: Around 100 members of Taipei’s LGBTQ+ community protested on Sunday after police raided a gay bar the previous day and detained 51 people, an unusual move
articles.body: Around 100 members of Taipei’s LGBTQ+ community protested on Sunday after police raided a gay bar the previous day and detained 51 people, an unusual move in Taiwan, which has long projected a liberal image and legal protections for sexual minorities.The protest came a day after police raided Commander D, a well-known gay bar in Taipei’s Wanhua district, taking 51 people in for questioning and arresting the bar’s owner. Police said they had acted on a search warrant over suspected “offences against public morality”.According to precinct spokesman Chen Yu-cheng, those detained were suspected of violating a law prohibiting “wantonly exposing one’s naked body or presenting a lascivious posture in a public place or publicly accessible place”.Protesters marched to the precinct police station on Sunday, where they voiced anger over the raid and questioned the police action.“They raided the place violently. It was very scary,” one of those detained told Reuters.The Taipei city government referred Reuters to a separate police statement saying officers had received a complaint alleging that the bar could be violating public decency laws.What happened at Commander D?The raid took place on October 3 at around 4.30 pm, according to local reports. The bar's manager protested the police action and was handcuffed, while people at the scene said officers initially refused to show the search warrant.Police later described the operation as questioning rather than a search, according to local reports, prompting further anger among those present.The reports also said a large number of customers who had removed their clothes were taken away for questioning. It was not immediately clear whether the operation was connected to a suspected drug offence.Commander D, which has operated in Taipei for about 14 years, had previously come under scrutiny after a city councillor raised concerns about alleged underage customers entering bars.The councillor had also released photographs of the bar's interior and alleged that underage youths were being subjected to inappropriate activities. The allegations prompted Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an to order an investigation.The bar denied having any system involving underage customers and said intimate interactions between customers were private behaviour. It said it had an identity and age-verification mechanism and checked customers' identification at entry.Taiwan's LGBTQ+ rights recordThe raid has drawn particular attention because Taiwan has positioned itself as one of Asia's most progressive societies on LGBTQ+ rights.Taiwan legalised same-sex marriage in 2019, becoming the first jurisdiction in Asia to do so. Taipei is also due to hold its main Pride event later this month, one of the largest such events in East Asia.Mayor Chiang, from the opposition Kuomintang, has previously attended Taipei Pride and expressed support for the LGBTQ+ community. He faces an election next month.The precinct chief, who did not give his name, briefly addressed protesters outside the police station.“We respect the culture of a pluralistic society and will protect the rights of every citizen,” he said, as protesters shouted their disapproval.A protestor shared that he was angry that the raid had taken place during Pride month.“I’m not cool with this,” he said. “This city used to claim that it was queer friendly.”You use AI every day. articles.title: A grandmother’s 23-year-old letter was found inside a library book; a stranger tracked down the person it was written to
articles.summary: A letter written by a grandmother on 23 August 2003 for her granddaughter's 16th birthday has found its way back to its owner after 23 years.
articles.body: A letter written by a grandmother on 23 August 2003 for her granddaughter's 16th birthday has found its way back to its owner after 23 years. Katie Slocum, 36, discovered the 132-word message inside an Ann Patchett novel, "State of Wonder", which she had taken from a little free library in Washington, D.C. She posted a callout on 26 February, and Jacqueline Roche, 38, recognised the cursive the next day. Roche had donated the book in 2022 without realising the letter was inside. The two women met the following weekend in Mount Pleasant and have since become friends.How was the recipient of the 23-year-old letter foundSlocum works as a programme manager at American University's School of International Service and as a server at Bar del Monte, a restaurant in her neighbourhood. According to the Washington Post, she described the effort as a "long shot". On 26 February, she posted the details on three D.C.-focused social media forums. She also asked Dan Silverman, who runs the neighbourhood blog PoPville under the name "Prince of Petworth", to issue a callout for Jackie, which he did promptly.The next day, Jacqueline Roche, 38, was scrolling through PoPville's Instagram posts when a headline about a lost letter caught her attention. She looked at the cursive in the photograph, saw to whom it was addressed and recognised it immediately. She had not realised until then that the letter was missing. She messaged PoPville to say she was the Jackie in question and that her paternal grandmother had given her the letter on her 16th birthday. Silverman replied a day later, asked for her email address and put her in touch with Slocum.What was special about Roche’s Sweet 16 celebrationRoche's parents held a large Sweet 16 party for her on 23 August 2003 at a catering hall in Bergen County, New Jersey, where she grew up. Dozens of friends and family attended. Following tradition, Roche named 16 people in her life, gave a short speech about each and lit a candle for each one. Her grandmother, Irene Roche, helped her light one of the last candles.Irene Roche, who had just celebrated her 90th birthday, grew up in the Bronx, raised two children and worked as a bookkeeper until retiring in her 70s. She was the first person to take her granddaughter across the Hudson River into New York, and she took her to her first Broadway show, "Beauty and the Beast", in the mid-1990s. She said she wrote the letter on a whim, wanting her granddaughter to know why she was proud of her. As one of 27 grandchildren herself, she said she had never felt special growing up.How did Roche lose the letter in 2022Roche kept the letter for years. It went with her to college in St. Augustine, Florida, and to her first teaching job in New Orleans. It then stayed at her childhood home in Bergen County for three years while she taught first grade in Brazil. She retrieved it in 2016 and took it to D.C., to Michigan for a graduate degree in educational leadership and policy, and back to D.C., where she settled in Mount Pleasant in 2019. She is almost certain she lost it in 2022, when she accidentally included it in books she gave away while moving in with her boyfriend. According to the Post, no one knows what happened to the letter between her donating it in 2022 and Slocum picking it up in 2024.Roche and Slocum met the weekend after Silverman made the introduction, at Mount Pleasant's town square near the farmers market. Slocum was holding the Patchett book. The two women hugged and talked for about 20 minutes. Roche told the Post she felt as though they were already friends. Irene Roche said friends at her senior community enjoyed the story, and that the letter's closing lines told her granddaughter to take whatever life gave her with both hands and "keep on dancing".You use AI every day. articles.title: Latin America’s conservative shift faces its biggest test yet in Brazil election
articles.summary: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva barely leads Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil election polls as analysts say the vote could reshape conservatism in the Americas.
articles.body: SÃO PAULO: As Brazil goes to the polls Sunday, analysts are watching closely to see whether the continent’s most populous nation will be the latest domino to fall into the conservative column, following Colombia, Peru, Chile and others, in voting out the left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Known by his nickname Lula, the 80-year-old, who served time in jail for corruption in a massive payback bribery scandal, barely leads Brazilian senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Going into Sunday’s first round, neither candidate is expected to win outright. The latest Datafolha poll puts Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 38%, with a two-point margin of error. If the election goes to a runoff, it has Lula up by 3%. But the polls have been wrong before. ANTI-CARTEL CANDIDATE 'THE TIGER' CHANNELS TRUMP AND BUKELE IN COLOMBIA ELECTION SHOCKER "The problem with Datafolha, which is the largest polling institute in the country, is that it tends to underestimate the force and voting intention in candidates running against Lula or the Workers Party (PT). This has been consistent for at least over a decade, and it underestimated Jair Bolsonaro’s number on the runoff of 2018 by 7%," Roberto Reis, an electoral strategist working with several candidates across multiple electoral tiers and analyzing aggregator data, told Fox News Digital. "According to the latest aggregator data such as MRT News or Polling Data, we currently have Lula leading Bolsonaro 42% to 39% on the first runoff of the elections with Bolsonaro leading Lula 45% to 44% on the runoff," he added. One Brazil analyst said the election is about more than just another ideological contest between left and right in Latin America. It is the single major remaining stumbling block in the Western Hemisphere that still hasn’t shifted to conservativism. While there are other left-wing governments in the hemisphere, including Cuba, Jamaica, Mexico, Nicaragua and Uruguay, Brazil is by far the largest and most important economy in this group with its status as the 11th largest world economy, according to the IMF, and the 10th largest world economy, according to the World Bank. ‘WAVE OF FREEDOM’ SWEEPS LATIN AMERICA AS TRUMP ALLY TAKES FIGHT TO MARXIST TERROR GROUP Bolsonaro has spent much of the campaign cultivating a relationship with President Donald Trump and presenting himself as a potential U.S. partner in the Western Hemisphere. He met Trump at the White House in May, where the two discussed organized crime, tariffs and Brazil's rare earth and critical mineral reserves — both critical prime-source materials Brazil has plenty of and which could significantly lower U.S. and European dependency on Russia and China. Bolsonaro also said he had asked Washington to designate Brazil's two largest criminal organizations, the First Capital Command (PCC, in its Portuguese acronym) and Red Command (Comando Vermelho, in Portuguese), as terrorist groups. Both designations were accepted by the Department of State on May 28 and became effective in June under section 219 of the Immigration and Naturalization Code. TRUMP ADMIN'S LIST OF US-DESIGNATED 'FOREIGN TERRORIST' GROUPS IN LATIN AMERICA EXPANDS TO 21 The designation by the U.S. government incensed Lula and his allies and was viewed as direct meddling in domestic affairs and a rubber stamp from the Trump administration that the left-wing, populist president has not been doing enough to combat organized crime in his country, directly favoring Bolsonaro’s contest in the elections. Flávio Bolsonaro has also proposed a free-trade agreement between Brazil and the United States, potentially expanding it into a broader free-trade arrangement among countries in the Americas. And his campaign has emphasized cooperation with Washington on critical minerals, an increasingly strategic issue as the Trump administration tries to reduce U.S. dependence on China, as per a current report by Brazil’s leading newspaper, Folha de S. Paulo. That would represent a significant change in emphasis from Lula's foreign policy. China is Brazil's largest trading partner, and Brazilian agricultural exports to China totaled more than $55 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. Lula has defended maintaining strong relations with Beijing while pursuing what he describes as an independent foreign policy that oftentimes borders on aggressiveness toward both the United States and its closest allies, such as Israel. Lula's relationship with Trump has been considerably more complicated. Washington imposed new 25% tariffs on a wide range of Brazilian goods in July, affecting about $7 billion of Brazilian exports, while Lula's government has challenged the measures and sought negotiations with Washington with very limited success so far. Washington has also imposed a ban on most new permanent visa requests coming from Brazil, and that could lead to green cards. TANVI RATNA: LATIN AMERICA'S RIGHT TURN IS REDRAWING THE UNITED STATES' BACKYARD A Bolsonaro presidency would come with stated plans for closer U.S. economic and security cooperation, greater alignment with Israel, a more confrontational posture toward China's influence in Brazil, and reduced friction both within the hemisphere and in global affairs. Whether those policies can all be implemented depends on negotiations with Congress, Brazil's powerful bureaucracy and the country's economic interests — especially the agribusiness and mining powerhouses in the country. A Lula victory would mean continuity in a foreign policy trajectory that seeks strong commercial ties with China while maintaining strategic autonomy from Washington, alongside his government's current position on Israel and Gaza. Both attitudes are in direct defiance of Trump’s policies and could end up damaging U.S.-Brazilian relations even further. articles.title: Drumcree: Sinn Féin will co-operate with PSNI over Drumcree protest
articles.summary: Protesters have remained on the Garvaghy Road since last Sunday as the fallout over the proposed Portadown District Orange Lodge march continues.
articles.body:
Sinn Féin will co-operate with the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) over any potential investigation into the protest on the Garvaghy Road, the party president has said.

Protesters have remained on the Garvaghy Road since Sunday 27 September as the fallout over the proposed Portadown District Orange Lodge march continues, and rallies on both sides of the dispute were held on Saturday.

Mary Lou McDonald has said that "there's no question with us co-operating with any process that will unfold".

Speaking on Sunday, Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson said police confirmed to them that Saturday's gathering on the Garvaghy Road was "unnotified" and police were "taking evidence".

McDonald and Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill are among those who have attended the protest, which police have described as unnotified and "therefore illegal".

The Portadown District has maintained a presence at Drumcree Church after talks to end the parading dispute ended without agreement on Thursday.

The Portadown District attempted to march again on Sunday morning.

The PSNI said that anyone "found to have broken the law will face criminal justice consequences".

However, speaking on the BBC's Sunday Politics programme , McDonald said: "There are moments in politically life where you have to take a stand, and this is one of those moments."

When asked about the legality of the protest she said: "Others will determine whether or not that is in fact the case."

The Parades Commission's decided that the parade - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - could go ahead on Sunday 27 September with restrictions.

A fresh legal bid by the residents to prevent the march was due to be heard on Friday - but has now been postponed until Monday.

Speaking of how many times the Portadown District have attempted to proceed with their march in the past week, Dawson told BBC News NI on Sunday: "I haven't been keeping a running check on it, but I think it's 15 times we have attempted to implement the determination issued by the Parades Commission and re-enforced by a High Court judge."

He said that "on each and every occasion the message from the PSNI headquarters is they are unable to offer us safe passage down the road".

"So we continue to be here waiting for the Chief Constable to apply the law to a lawful determination," Dawson said.

"Obviously I'm not involved in policing matters and we respect the police but I suspect that time is running out, that he can't continue to say that he is unable to his job."

Dawson said Portadown remains a "very determined district".

"Some of us have been here for the last 28 years each and every Sunday, and we are happy to allow the law to take its course but the law needs to be implemented and it needs to be respected by everybody across the communities."

The actions of McDonald, O'Neill and others have received condemnation including from members of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP).

In a post on social media, deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said the "behaviour of Michelle O'Neill and her party has been disgraceful" and a "complete abdication of leadership".

McDonald said that this "comes down to right and wrong", and that as people who care passionately about the future, her and O'Neill know that for "that to happen we have to stand four square with the community of the Garvaghy Road".

She said there was a "broad crowd politically and otherwise" at the rally on Saturday, adding that it was "resolute but good humoured with a real eye for the future".

"I cannot fathom anybody suggesting that 28 years on when progress has been made in such significant ways, not least in Portadown and in the wider Garvaghy community, why it is that anybody would seek to reopen that wound."

Meanwhile, in response to DUP leader Gavin Robinson's comments that Sinn Féin is attempting to goad unionists into collapsing Stormont, McDonald said it is "anything but", adding that it is about the ability of communities to live work, and build futures together.

Speaking to BBC News NI at Drumcree on Saturday, DUP MP Carla Lockhart said there could be "repercussions for a very long time if mob rule wins over the rule of law".

"No, we need the police service to step up and do their job. I do think if the real residents step forward we can and should discuss further options and resolutions, because we do want to see this resolved," Lockhart said.

McDonald said that "the real voices of the Garvaghy Road" have called for support and people to come stand for them and "my god have they had a response, not just in Ireland but right across the world".

McDonald said her party has pressed Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant and Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin.

She said that "we have found ourselves landed in this situation by an utterly reckless determination by the Parades Commission".

McDonald added that Martin and her both agree that the Parade's Commission determination as "incomprehensible and wrong".

Speaking at a Fianna Fáil dinner on Saturday, Martin said that "absolutely nobody benefits from the reopening of the dispute over the parade on the Garvaghy Road".

Sir Chris said he was "concerned at the prolonged standoff" which he said was "ultimately in nobody's interests".

"I have been working with all those involved to find a mutually acceptable solution," he said in a social media post, on Saturday.

McDonald said the resolution is that Sir Chris needs to "call this, make it clear that he puts a stop to this march and thereby creates the space for a mediation".

Elsewhere on Sunday, a number of people carried a cross from Drumcree Parish Church to St Mark's Church in Portadown under the 'Carry the Cross Initiative'.

The organisers are appealing for "healing, unity and genuine reconciliation across Portadown, pointing to the unifying message of the cross of Christ to break decades of division".

Organisers said the initiative has been "strictly curtailed following a ruling by the Parades Commission", which limits the gathering the fewer than 10 people and alters the original route.

Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision that was upheld for the past 28 years.

The row re-emerged last month after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission was overturned, and a fresh application to parade was lodged.

Last Friday, the commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place.

However, that decision was challenged in several Belfast courts on Saturday, before finally being given the go-ahead just hours before it was due to take place.

articles.title: Spain protests flare after housing bill rejected: Will it cause snap poll?
articles.summary: Measures pushed by Spain’s leftist government fail to pass parliament as the protests spread.
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of people have rallied across Spain as protests have spread since the conservative-dominated parliament rejected a bill proposing measures to tackle a housing crisis.

Parliament on Friday voted down two decrees proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority left-wing coalition government that were intended to address the housing crisis.

The protests erupted late last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home of 70 years in the capital, Madrid. Maria del Carmen Abascal’s eviction came after an international investment fund bought her building and hiked the rent.

Local media reports have suggested that Sanchez could call snap elections for as early as November after watching the strength of Saturday’s protests across the country. Spain’s current legislative term is set to end next summer.

Will the housing crisis trigger snap elections? Here’s what we know:

The emergency measures proposed by Spain’s leftist government to tackle the country’s housing affordability crisis failed to pass on Friday.

The government had proposed two measures to protect renters in the country. The first decree was meant to stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder, impose tighter restrictions on short-term leases and provide tax incentives to encourage renting and the construction of housing.

The second decree proposed making leases automatically renew when they are set to expire, essentially making them indefinite. A property owner would have to pay a tenant 12 months of rent to break the contract.

Sanchez, who leads a coalition government composed of his Socialist Party and the far-left Sumar, ⁠appealed to lawmakers in the run-up to the vote to put aside political calculations and pressure.

“Think about ordinary people, about those who most need the protection of public institutions. Think about the millions of young people who ⁠cannot afford to ⁠move out of their parents’ homes. Think about the families living with the constant ⁠anxiety of ever-rising rents,” he said before the voting.

But his government’s proposed measures were shot down by the majority of ⁠the 350-seat lower house of parliament.

The right-wing ⁠Catalan separatist ⁠party Junts refused to back the housing decrees, saying they would ultimately tighten the housing market. The centre-right Popular Party and far-right Vox also voted against the measures.

Miriam Nogueras of Junts argued the decrees would lead only to owners removing their properties from the rental market and thus driving up prices even further.

“If they really wanted to protect people, collar the vulture funds, and reactivate housing, they would have already done it. They’ve had eight years,” she added on X, referring to Sanchez’s government.

Health Minister Monica Garcia said on X that the right-wing parties “have voted for a feudal economy in which a minority extracts the salary from a majority that works for their luxuries. And they do it against their own voters, who also suffer increasingly high rents, live in fear that the contract will end and can even be evicted.”

“Today the right has given rent-seeking a parliamentary majority that it doesn’t have on the street, but it’s going to pay for it sooner rather than later,” she added.

Before the parliamentary vote, Marta Soler Gallart, head of the Department of Sociology at the University of Barcelona, explained that neither of the two decrees addressed the housing problem in the medium or long term.

“Models such as Vienna’s with its low rents are cited in support of these decrees, but it is overlooked that the Vienna model and others have low rents because of their long history of creating and maintaining public social housing,” Soler Gallart told Al Jazeera on September 30.

“In Spain, however, public funds are invested in social housing which, after a while, the recipients sell at market price.”

Soler Gallart also said the new measures disadvantage landlords with small or few properties by extending five-year tenancy agreements by a further two years and by providing an indefinite extension of their leases.

“However, these extensions are not compulsory if the landlord can prove that they need the property for their own use,” she said.

Protests erupted across Spain in late September after 87-year-old Abascal was evicted from her home. The investment fund that bought her building hiked her rent by more than 200 percent to roughly $1,880 a month, a move aimed at pushing out the long-term tenant to make way for lucrative tourist apartments.

In recent years, Spain has seen protests against mass tourism, which has been linked to the housing crisis and soaring cost of living. Spain is the second most visited country in the world, attracting 97 million tourists last year.

While Abascal has returned to her home, according to her representatives, she has become the face of the country’s housing crisis, and people across Spain have been demanding the government address the issue.

Angered by parliament’s rejection of the government measures, tens of thousands of people took to the streets.

“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined Saturday’s protest in Madrid, told the Reuters news agency.

“It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”

While the protests were mostly peaceful, in the southeastern city of Valencia, police fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up demonstrations. About 30 protesters managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building, before police removed them.

Meanwhile, in Madrid, Spanish police arrested three members of a far-right group and fired rubber bullets on Saturday night.

Far-right activists, some of whom performed Nazi salutes, tried to reach demonstrators camped out in the Puerta del Sol, a central square in the Spanish capital, the Spanish government said.

Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants’ Union, said Saturday’s rallies revealed “a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time and energy that is showing that eight days of people’s power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government”.

“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” Racu added.

Housing is a sensitive issue in Spain because it impacts how people vote. The average rent in the country has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square metre has risen from 8.20 euros (about $9.08 at the time) in 2016 to 15.1 euros ($17.15) this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.

In an October 1 article for Vanity Fair, Spanish journalist Jorge Dioni Lopez noted that after eight years in power, housing is what is causing Sanchez to lose support among educated young people, children of the middle classes.

“The government faces a difficult situation. Firstly, because most of the relevant powers lie with other levels of government. Secondly, because Spain is a nation of homeowners. Unlike in other European countries, almost all the public housing that has been built has ended up in private hands, and historically, homeownership has been more attractive than renting,” he wrote.

“Housing is our savings system and also the primary means of transmitting wealth between generations,” he added.

After Spain’s parliament rejected the government’s housing reform bills on Friday, the leader of the centre-right People’s Party, (PP) Alberto Nunez Feijoo, urged Sanchez to “call elections as soon as possible”, claiming he had the support of “neither the streets nor parliament”.

While Sanchez has not officially announced new elections, the Spanish online news site El Diario has reported that elections could take place as early as November 29. Spain’s general elections are currently scheduled for July 2027.

articles.title: Porridge gurus from opposite sides of globe triumph in world championship
articles.summary: Dutch champion Gina Saarberg took the coveted Golden Spurtle, while Australian champion maestro Rob Reid won the Speciality Porridge category at the finals in the Scottish Highlands.
articles.body:
Two national porridge-making champions from almost opposite sides of the planet have triumphed in the annual world championships held in the Scottish Highlands.

Gina Saarberg, 28, took the coveted Golden Spurtle using the same recipe that saw her crowned Dutch champion in July, using organic pinhead oats, salt and water that she brought with her from the Netherlands.

Australian champion Rob Reid took the speciality award - where competitors can combine oatmeal with any ingredients - with his porridge cannoli, an oaty spin on a tube-shaped dessert that originated in Sicily.

Thirty competitors from 14 countries took part in the contest, held each year at Carrbridge, just north of Aviemore.

What's a golden spurtle and why do so many people want one?

Norwegian oats win world porridge championship

Gina, from Zuthphen, started eating a kind of porridge using rolled oats in her student days because it was a cheap meal.

But she had never tasted the traditional variety until she learned about the Dutch porridge-making contest and decided to enter as a "bit of a joke".

"When I first tasted it, it was a world of difference - I've been missing out all these years," she told BBC Scotland News.

The contest rules only allow three ingredients - oats, water and salt.

She only started adding salt to her porridge ahead of the competition, but quickly realised it "really brings out the nuances and different aromas".

She believes her secret weapon may have been the water which she brought with her from her home city.

"It's very soft, and I think the mineral content may have something to do with it. I'm not sure - but it worked last time and this time as well, so maybe it's the water".

In the Speciality Porridge category, Rob, from Sydney, came up with his recipe just a few weeks before competing in the Australian national porridge championships - the Pearly Spurtle - after realising how seriously everyone was taking it.

Tapping into his family heritage - his father is Scottish and his mother is Sicilian - he decided to make a porridge cannoli.

"I then had to engineer it," the 36-year-old told BBC Scotland News.

The cream uses the traditional mix of ricotta, mascarpone and sugar but he blended in porridge, sieved it and added some ground toasted oats.

It provides the filling for shells, made like brandy snaps but using Sicilian Marsala wine instead.

"After I came up with the idea, I spent a whole day in the kitchen with one of my daughters at home making multiple different types of shells and different creams, trying to work out how to put the porridge in the cream," he said.

Having won the Pearly Spurtle, he then spent the next six weeks improving the recipe in preparation for the ultimate challenge in Scotland.

Rob used to own a café, but he now installs blinds and curtains for a living and uses his free time to channel his culinary creativity.

"Not working in a kitchen for something like this meant I was able to be really creative with it because it wasn't my job and I was able to play with it a bit more," he said.

The annual contest was started in 1994 in Carrbridge by a local hotel owner as a way of promoting the health benefits of porridge as well raising the profile of the area.

Porridge Chieftain Alan Rankin said: "The World Porridge Making Championship is a wonderfully quirky tradition that thrives on good humour and friendly competition, offering a wonderful escape from the daily grind.

"Each year, our local community opens its doors and we hope everyone who joined us leaves with fond memories of their visit."

articles.title: Where will India be 5 to 10 years from now? EAM Jaishankar answers
articles.summary: External affairs minister S Jaishankar said India has the potential to move rapidly up the global power hierarchy over the next five to 10 years, citing
articles.body: External affairs minister S Jaishankar said India has the potential to move rapidly up the global power hierarchy over the next five to 10 years, citing decades of high growth ahead, a supportive demographic profile and the emergence of new economic opportunities.Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi on Sunday, Jaishankar was asked where India would be positioned in the global order five to 10 years from now. He said countries currently classified as middle powers would not necessarily follow the same trajectory.“Some powers are more middle, and some are upper middle,” Jaishankar said. “Some of the powers have considerable and realistic potential even in the near short medium term to grow very rapidly.”Turning to India, Jaishankar said the country has “decades of high growth” ahead and argued that its demographic profile could help sustain that growth.“In the case of India, because we have decades of high growth ahead of us, and we have all said and done, a demography that will sustain that growth,” he said.Jaishankar also argued that India may not need to follow the traditional industrialisation path taken by earlier economies, pointing to the emergence of new possibilities in a rapidly changing global economy.“I would even argue, a world that is much more creative, where many new possibilities are there, so that we don't necessarily have to tread the earlier path of industrialization,” he said.“The orthodox path will have to devise something much more contemporary for what awaits us,” he added.India’s place among middle powersJaishankar said the global power hierarchy is likely to evolve unevenly, with countries currently grouped together as middle powers potentially moving in different directions.“Among the middle powers, some will peel off, some will stay put, some may drop down a bit,” he said.“That is the reality. That will be part of the evolution of the global order,” Jaishankar added.His remarks came during a wider discussion on the changing international power structure at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi. The meeting is being held on October 4 and 5 and brings together senior decision-makers and experts to discuss foreign and security policy issues.Jaishankar’s wider power assessmentEarlier during the discussion, Jaishankar said the United States and China should not be viewed as middle powers, highlighting their vastly different levels of global influence.“When we say what the prospects are, we are also looking at an international landscape. As I said, what is important to define is what is not a middle power,” he said.On the US, Jaishankar said Washington has been the “underwriter of the global system for many decades” and has “a significant lead over any other power”.He then pointed to China’s economic strength, saying it accounts for “one third of the global manufacturing” and that its economic capabilities are translating into political influence.“This is really, in a sense, the subject matter of our discussion,” Jaishankar said.The Munich Leaders Meeting is a platform organised by the Munich Security Conference, a leading international forum on security and foreign policy. articles.title: Is the Sudanese army gaining momentum against the RSF?
articles.summary: The SAF claims victory in a vital North Kordofan town, weakening RSF’s access to fighters and supply routes.
articles.body:
Sudan’s army has made gains in the war against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary in recent weeks as it tries to gain the upper hand in the three-and-a-half-year war that has ravaged one of the poorest countries in the world.

The Sudanese armed forces (SAF) on Friday said its soldiers captured the town of al-Mazroub after fierce fighting. The town is one of the RSF’s most important positions in North Kordofan, and its capture extends a series of military successes in a region that has become a central battleground in the civil war.

The SAF has pushed the RSF out of much of the state, increasing pressure on the paramilitary group’s positions and supply routes.

But the wider war remains far from settled, with the RSF still controlling almost all of Darfur and parts of Kordofan.

Sudan’s civil war erupted in April 2023 in the capital, Khartoum, after months of tensions between the SAF and the RSF. The conflict has since expanded to 13 of Sudan’s 18 states and has displaced 14 million people, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises .

So what are the latest gains made by the Sudanese army? And is it gaining the upper hand?

The capture of al-Mazroub on Friday is the latest advance for the army in North Kordofan.

“The Sudanese army has taken full control of al-Mazroub after battles with the Rapid Support Forces,” Mohamed Deidan, spokesman for the army’s special forces, told the Anadolu news agency.

Deidan described the capture as an important step in the army’s efforts to cut the RSF’s supply lines, saying the town serves as a link between army-controlled North Kordofan and West Kordofan, which is an RSF stronghold.

He called the advance a major turning point in the fighting in the Kordofan region.

Fighting across Kordofan has intensified since late 2025 after the RSF captured el-Fasher, the army’s last major stronghold in Darfur.

Meanwhile, on Saturday, the Sudanese army announced it had delivered a “knockout blow” to the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), in Blue Nile state, claiming to have inflicted heavy losses on fighters and equipment. SPLM-N controls parts of South Kordofan.

In a statement, the army’s Fourth Infantry Division said its troops, backed by supporting forces, targeted the two groups in the Minza and Bashkarkad areas.

The operation inflicted “heavy losses in lives and equipment”, disrupted their movements and thwarted attempts to advance towards army positions, the statement said.

There was no immediate comment from the RSF.

However, separately on Saturday, Blue Nile Governor Ahmed al-Omda Badi said the RSF launched drone attacks on the governor’s house but the aircraft were intercepted by air defences. He did not give details about any casualties or damage from the attack.

Again, the RSF has not commented on this government statement.

Blue Nile in southeastern Sudan has witnessed a military escalation in recent days with the RSF and SPLM-N launching attacks on several areas in the state.

What areas do the Sudanese army and RSF control?

The SAF controls Khartoum and most of the country’s north, east and centre while the RSF controls much of western Sudan, including almost all of Darfur and parts of Kordofan.

South Kordofan remains contested while the SPLM-N holds pockets of territory in the south.

The balance has changed significantly during the war. The army recovered Khartoum and other areas in central Sudan after suffering major losses early in the conflict.

But the RSF’s capture of el-Fasher in October 2025 cemented its control over Darfur and shifted the main front eastwards towards the Kordofan region.

According to an Al Jazeera analysis of data from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), an independent conflict monitor, about 19.7 percent of all of the war’s recorded attacks have taken place in the Kordofan area, putting the region second only to Khartoum.

In July, the International Organization for Migration said the number of people newly displaced across Kordofan had risen by nearly two-thirds since February to more than 219,000.

What is the humanitarian situation on the ground?

The shifting front lines have done little to ease Sudan’s humanitarian catastrophe.

About 19.5 million people – more than 40 percent of the population – were facing acute hunger while 14 areas in North Darfur, South Darfur and South Kordofan were at risk of famine, the United Nations-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification hunger monitor said in May.

About 825,000 children were projected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year, it added.

In September, the Sudanese pound had lost nearly half its value in army-held territory since the beginning of the summer, putting basic goods beyond the reach of many families.

articles.title: Exclusive: Trump envoy blasts South Africa over hateful ‘kill' chant, says country is drifting toward US foes
articles.summary: U.S. Ambassador Brent Bozell warns South Africa is drifting toward Iran, Russia, China and Hamas as Trump pushes back on land seizure policies.
articles.body: JOHANNESBURG: The U.S. ambassador to South Africa has hit out at the country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, telling Fox News Digital, "You've got a president of South Africa who refuses to condemn an incitement to kill." Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III was responding strongly, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, to being summoned this past week to South Africa’s foreign ministry and criticized for "undiplomatic conduct." This is the third time the ambassador has received a démarche — a diplomatic rebuke — from Pretoria in the nine months since he arrived here. The ambassador has been slammed by South Africa for relaying President Donald Trump’s condemnation of South African policies and statements. Bozell is a former Fox News contributor and founder of the largest conservative media watchdog, the Media Research Center. TRUMP ADMIN IMPOSES NEW VISA RESTRICTIONS OVER ALLEGED RACIAL DISCRIMINATION, LAND SEIZURES IN SOUTH AFRICA He has repeatedly pushed for issues brought up by President Trump in a testy confrontation in the Oval Office with Ramaphosa 16 months ago to be addressed. Among other points, these include alleged race-based discrimination, allegations of murder and torture of farmers, plans for uncompensated land seizures, and the incitement of violence against minority groups. The ambassador said three of the five specific "asks" the Trump administration wants have been ignored by South Africa. High up the list is President Trump’s demand that Ramaphosa stop people in South Africa from shouting "Kill the Boer! Kill the farmer!" A Boer is a White man, according to the Merriam-Webster dictionary. It defines it as "a South African of Dutch or Huguenot descent". Ramaphosa has claimed he can’t stop people chanting this slogan because it’s been cleared for use by the country’s supreme court. Bozell told Fox News Digital, "You've got a president of South Africa who refuses to condemn an incitement to kill." SOUTH AFRICA’S ILLEGAL MIGRATION BACKLASH MIRRORS POLITICAL BATTLES ACROSS THE WEST He added, "You've got a government that has said it's not going to do any more for the Afrikaner rural community, and it's got a government that's saying no, your mining has to go through race-based programs. We're not going to allow your investments to go the way everyone else has been allowed to go". "Those were three strikes and you're out as far as we were concerned," Bozell said. "Ask 100% of the world if 'kill the farmer, kill the Boer' isn’t hate speech," he continued. "If that isn't hate speech, I don't know what hate speech is: inciting people to commit murder. So the answer we've gotten is, well, the court said it isn't. To which our response is look, in the United States, the president can disagree with the court and does about every five minutes because that's what you do in a democracy when you disagree with something." TRUMP GETS MAJOR WIN AGAINST CHINA IN AFRICAN RARE EARTH MINERALS RACE Bozell added, "So, to say, well, you can't do it because the court said it's not, you know, that's poppycock. If President Ramaphosa, if he wants to, he can do it. It's just as simple as that." The ambassador pushed hard on the point, saying "How hard is it to say this chant, where some, where people do it, 50,000 people in the stadium jump up and down, pantomiming guns, shooting people, how hard is it to say, stop it? This is awful that anybody would be inciting people to kill." South Africa, analysts say, is drawing ever closer to Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba. The African National Congress, the ANC, the party which rules the country in the so-called "government of national unity." has hosted the terror group Hamas. This is very much on the administration’s radar. President Trump met with Bozell in Washington again recently, with the ambassador telling Fox News Digital the president’s thinking "perhaps most of all, he's concerned about how South Africa has been systematically leaving the non-alignment space and moving closer and closer to our adversaries." Referring to South Africa, the ambassador added, "There are people who are living in the glory days of the Soviet Union, and they want to go back to the good old days of communism. Why are they still working with Cuba?" Digging deeper, Bozell asked, "Why are they working with Iran and Hamas terror organizations? What's Russia doing for them? What's China doing for them? This is bad news when they're going in that direction. What we're saying is simply do what you've always done. Have a non-aligned with both sides. We'll live with that." US COUNTERS CHINA AS BEIJING’S ‘SHOCK WAVE’ HITS AFRICAN ECONOMIES The ambassador stressed that the U.S. wants to make dynamic business with South Africa on mining, particularly on critical or rare earth minerals. He stated, "We're not going to do what the Chinese do. They come in, they take the ore, they take it to China, they benefit [from] it and they make a pile of money. We're saying to South Africa, we'll come in, we'll do the mining, we'll do it right there in South Africa." He continued, "South Africa gets the money, not the Chinese. We bring in the technology that they could never have. We've created hundreds of thousands of jobs. We're saying we could create more and more and more at a time when they desperately need it, but it will be good for us as well. This is the partnership we want." Elon Musk and his Starlink satellite internet company are one of many U.S. companies which want to enter South Africa. But in the telecommunications and mining fields, the government insists that 30% of foreign company ownership must be given to Black local entrepreneurs. Bozell says this is problematical for the U.S. "There are literally billions of dollars from American firms and American government investments ready to go into mining, but it's not going to go there so long as you have these race-based avenues they must go through. In telecom, Elon Musk has said he will put Starlink in 500 schools and pay for it in perpetuity if he's allowed to go this way. And they said, 'No, we want 30% of your company.' So yeah, of course it's hurting." On Friday, a senior official at South Africa’s Department of International Relations – the country’s foreign ministry – confirmed to Fox News Digital that they demarched Ambassador Bozell for a third time, adding, "This is a record. He was called in to explain his undiplomatic conduct. The issues related to the bilateral relations between the two countries are a subject of ongoing discussions. There is commitment from both sides to resolve the outstanding matters. South Africa values the relationship with the USA. It is a mutually beneficial partnership." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Also, Friday, a State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "We are not interested in diplomatic maneuvering, procedural delays or dialogue for dialogue’s sake. The ball is now squarely in the Government of South Africa’s court to outline the relationship it wants with the United States and respond accordingly to President Trump’s executive order." Still, Bozell looks to the future of the U.S.-South Africa relationship with guarded optimism. "Look, temperatures can go up, but I want their temperature to go down too. You know, we want this partnership. We want to figure this out. It's good for South Africa. It's good for the United States of America. Temperatures need to go down, and we got to figure it out."

articles.title: Mother aiming to get kid's book in paediatric cancer units
articles.summary: She is hoping Edie's Magic Hair can be distributed to hospitals to help other children losing their hair.
articles.body:
A mother who wrote a book to help her toddler cope with losing her hair during cancer treatment is hoping that copies can be distributed to hospitals to help other children going through the same thing.

Holly, who used to live in Bristol but relocated to London, wrote Edie's Magic Hair about a young girl who has to regrow her hair in a last step to become a superhero.

The titular character was inspired by her four-year-old daughter Edie, who was diagnosed with a rare form of bone cancer last year. She is now in remission.

Holly says that because the book worked for her daughter, it could "have that same positive impact for children in and around her age going through exactly the same thing".
