Holly said Edie had been "frightened" at the sight of her hair falling out so quickly after starting treatment.

She added the children's hospital where Edie was treated had some good distractions such as play areas, but nothing to distract from the physical impacts of chemotherapy.

Following Edie's successful treatment and remission, Holly launched a crowdfunder to support the production and distribution of the book to specialist paediatric cancer wards around the country.

She said: "The book was first and foremost for Edie in that moment. She needed something, she needed a vehicle, she needed a bridge to understand what was going on in a way that allowed her to escape."

She added she believed the story could "give hope" and "pride" to other children going through cancer treatment, just like it did for Edie.

articles.title: Russia hits Kyiv bridge as Germany’s Merz visits Ukraine’s capital
articles.summary: German chancellor visits Kyiv amid air raid sirens, pledging strong support as Russian strikes disrupt the capital.
articles.body:
Russia has struck a key bridge in Kyiv just as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The unannounced visit, marked by the sound of air sirens and explosions, came on Sunday to underscore Germany’s support for the nation at a time when Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities are increasing.

In a written statement, Merz said he “travelled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks”.

“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.

Merz and Zelenskyy met at the National Academy of Sciences, which was struck by a Russian drone on September 28.

Zelenskyy told Merz that Kyiv’s citizens are going through “terrible nights and days” due to the ongoing Russian attacks.

Merz was accompanied by his economy minister, as well as executives from several large German companies, such as Siemens Energy and Diehl Defence.

Ukraine and Germany are also expected to finalise a deal to produce drones and other weapons together that can travel more than 600 miles (965.6km) in an effort to strike deeper into Russia.

Germany has been one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters. In April, the two countries signed a military pact worth more than $4bn. On Sunday, a $1.1bn military aid package is set to be announced, alongside $394m to repair damage to Ukraine’s energy sector.

Merz’s visit comes a day after Russia warned foreign diplomats and nationals to leave the capital to avoid getting hurt.

Russia’s Ministry of Defence promised to intensify strikes on Ukraine after Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Reuters news agency that it is doubling down on targeting Russian oil refineries after several civilians were killed and wounded over the weekend.

The strike that hit the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River on Sunday also damaged a road and the supply of hot water in the area, according to a social media statement from Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. It is the second bridge in the capital to be hit this weekend.

Russia’s all-out war on Ukraine is in its fifth year. Both sides have increased the number of drone and missile attacks on infrastructure, logistics and military sites in recent months.

articles.title: Daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians still at risk
articles.summary: Katie Amess questions if anything has changed to protect politicians five years after her father's death.
articles.body:
The daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians are still at risk and questioned if anything has changed five years after her father's death.

Katie Amess told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg what happened to her father "wasn't an isolated incident, we are seeing increased threats towards members of parliament".

Sir David was the Conservative MP for Southend West when he was stabbed multiple times while holding a constituency surgery in Leigh-on-Sea, Essex, in October 2021.

The government commissioned a review into his death in August , to identify lessons to be learned and recommend steps to minimise the risk of future tragedies.

The review is being led by former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland, with the aim of reporting within six months.

The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years since the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe in July this year, Sir David's murder in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox's murder in 2016.

The five years since her father was killed have been "absolutely devastating and heartbreaking", his daughter told Kuenssberg, adding: "It's a very, very real situation that we're living with."

She has previously called for a public inquiry into the safety of politicians so people can have "the full facts to hand, full openness, honesty, and transparency".

The nearing anniversary of Sir David's murder comes after the man accused of murdering Widdecombe was also charged with preparing acts of terror, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Amess, who knew Widdecombe as a family friend and called her Aunt Ann, said: "It's absolutely so tragic and heartbreaking that now she isn't here either."

She added: "My dad was murdered five years ago so if so much has changed why are we still seeing other members of parliament or former members of parliament being targeted like this."

Widdecombe was not a sitting member of parliament when she died, but was a member of the Conservative Party and the member for Maidstone and the Weald from 1987 to 2010. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019.

Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family.

Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29.

"I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this," she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it".

Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be".

"We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'."

Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop."

She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat.

His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016.

A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments.

articles.title: Indian-origin US lawmaker Raja Krishnamoorthi introduces bills to help immigrant doctors, nurses
articles.summary: Indian-origin US lawmaker Raja Krishnamoorthi, along with Congressman Adam Smith, has introduced two bills aimed at helping immigrant and internationally
articles.body: Indian-origin US lawmaker Raja Krishnamoorthi, along with Congressman Adam Smith, has introduced two bills aimed at helping immigrant and internationally trained healthcare professionals overcome licensing and training barriers and join the US healthcare workforce amid rising shortages of medical workers.The Immigrants in Nursing and Allied Health Act and the Internationally Trained Physicians Assistance Act, introduced by Democratic Representatives Raja Krishnamoorthi and Adam Smith, would provide support for training, licensing and certification for immigrants seeking healthcare careers, including doctors trained outside the US.Smith said thousands of qualified healthcare professionals are unable to use their skills in the US because of licensing barriers, even as patients face longer waits for care.“We have thousands of skilled nurses, doctors, and health professionals in this country whose training and expertise are going to waste because their professional expertise is not recognized and they face numerous barriers to achieving the needed licensure,” Smith said.What the bills proposeThe Immigrants in Nursing and Allied Health Act would create grants for programmes offering training, licensing, certification and case management to immigrants seeking healthcare careers. It would also expand eligibility for the National Health Service Corps to immigrants who are not US citizens.The legislation covers several healthcare professions, including nursing, dental hygiene, dietetics, medical technology, occupational therapy, physical therapy, respiratory therapy and speech-language pathology. The statement said about 200,000 nurses would need to be hired each year to meet growing demand and replace retiring workers.The second bill, the Internationally Trained Physicians Assistance Act, would encourage states to create temporary licensing programmes allowing foreign-trained doctors to work under supervision while completing requirements for a US medical licence. It would also establish guaranteed residency positions for internationally trained physicians serving mainly medically underserved communities.Grants under the proposal would help eligible doctors with financial need cover costs related to exam preparation, testing, certification, English-language classes and case management.Why US lawmakers are pushing the billsThe lawmakers cited both healthcare workforce shortages and the underemployment of highly educated immigrants. A 2022 Migration Policy Institute study cited in the statement found that 2.1 million college-educated immigrants were unemployed or underemployed. The Association of American Medical Colleges has projected a shortage of up to 48,000 primary care physicians by 2034.Krishnamoorthi said the proposals would help qualified immigrants overcome barriers while allowing communities to make better use of skilled professionals already living in the US.The legislation has been endorsed by several organisations, including the International Medical Graduates Academy, Nashi Immigrants Health Board, Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, Sea Mar Community Health Center, Seattle Indian Health Board, Upwardly Global and World Education Services.You use AI every day. Lance Cpl. articles.title: After San Francisco's 1906 disaster, engineers blasted a 4,233-foot tunnel beneath the city; the hidden conduit still runs near Lands End
articles.summary: When the earthquake of 18 April 1906 struck San Francisco, the four-day fire that followed destroyed about 28,000 buildings and killed at least 3,000
articles.body: When the earthquake of 18 April 1906 struck San Francisco, the four-day fire that followed destroyed about 28,000 buildings and killed at least 3,000 people. The disaster prompted an overhaul of the city's water supply and wastewater collection. Among the results was the Mile Rock Tunnel, a 4,233 ft sewer and stormwater drain beneath the streets near Sutro Heights. Specified in 1914 by city engineer Michael Maurice O'Shaughnessy, it required workers to blast through more than 900 ft of solid rock and used compressed air to place concrete, a first successful application in San Francisco for the city. It went into operation by September 1915.Why was San Francisco’s 4,233-foot tunnel builtAccording to the American Society of Civil Engineers, Nemo cites Carl E. Grunsky, a former city engineer, who said that city officials and committees had pointed to the need for a comprehensive sewer system with increasing frequency before the earthquake. The city appointed a board of civil engineers in September 1892 to develop a cohesive system. Grunsky recorded that sewers at the time emptied into San Francisco Bay wherever they reached the water. He described one spot, where sewage ebbed and flowed with no rain to dilute it during half the year, as a "filthy nuisance beggaring description".Nemo reports that funding was limited, so the improvements Grunsky and his colleagues envisaged arrived in stages. Only in May 1908 did residents approve a $4 million sewer bond to pay for a larger number of changes, some of which would eventually cover the Mile Rock Tunnel. In 1912, Mayor "Sunny Jim" Rolph appointed Michael Maurice O'Shaughnessy as city engineer. O'Shaughnessy submitted his specifications for the tunnel to the Board of Public Works, which approved them in January 1914. The contract went to builder Edward Malley the following month for $193,314, but it fell apart after newspapers reported that Malley had not known the city would require indemnity insurance. By early 1915 the contract was held by R.C. Storrie and Co., run by the Scotsmen R.C. Storrie and Robert Muir.How was the 4,233-foot tunnel blasted through solid rockNemo, drawing on Mary L. Maniery's 1995 Historic American Engineering Record (HAER) report, explains that crews worked at both ends of the tunnel, digging towards each other. They had to cut through more than 900 ft of solid rock, using drilling and dynamite. The southern team worked through blue shale, creating eight to 11 holes with hand drills before each round of dynamite. In the north, where workers met blue sandstone before reaching blue shale, 17 to 21 holes from column-mounted piston drills were needed before each blast. A side-dump car on a narrow-gauge track, pulled by mules, carried the muck out. In stretches without rock, about 2,600 ft, timber cribbing provided support.Miners and shovelers worked two eight-hour shifts at either end, and the third shift each day was for concreting. Western Engineering (January 1915) reported an "average of 10 ft per day" at each end. According to Maniery's HAER report, the tunnel was the first successful application in San Francisco of pneumatic mixing and placing of concrete using compressed air. A compressor at the south end supplied the air, and materials were fed into a mixer at the tunnel adit. The mixed concrete flowed from a 6 in. pipe into a 6 in. rubber hose, and the teams communicated by a system of bells. Maniery wrote that an average of 32 batches per hour were placed even when the distance from the mixer to the discharge point was as great as 2,000 ft.When did the 4,233-foot tunnel near Lands End openNemo reports that the final section, roughly 30% of the total length, required cut-and-cover construction through sand. A dragline excavator and a turntable derrick rig excavated a trench the width of the street above. Groundwater kept flooding the trench, so a layer of gravel was laid at the bottom and the water was directed to two sumps through a 10 in. underdrain. According to the HAER report, this removed 1.25 million gallons of water every day. On 26 August 1915, an inspection party that included Rolph, O'Shaughnessy and Muir drove a car into the tunnel. The tunnel went into operation by September 1915. By 2 March 1916, according to a letter from O'Shaughnessy to the Board of Public Works, only the filling of a shaft and some pavement restoration remained, and these were finished by early June.Nemo states that O'Shaughnessy singled out Mile Rock in his 1922 summary of city construction in The Military Engineer, when the city had spent a total of $9 million on its new sewer system. A weir wall built in the mid-1990s means the tunnel now serves only as an emergency overflow. Tidal sand has reduced its cross-section, and by the time the weir was added, the tunnel was only about 3 ft tall within about 110 ft of the exit. Nemo concludes that the tunnel was innovative in its use of pneumatics for concrete placement, and that it was the first in the city built with both rock boring and open-cut timber cribbing.You use AI every day. articles.title: Yemen government announces major operation to retake Houthi territory
articles.summary: The Yemeni president's announcement comes amid an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.
articles.body:
Yemen's Saudi-backed government has announced a major military operation to retake territory from the Iran-backed Houthis.

It comes after an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in recent days. On Sunday, the Houthis said they had struck sites belonging to Saudi national oil company Aramco.

The group said the attack was in response to what it described as 50 Saudi-led coalition air and missile strikes in Yemen in 12 hours. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment.

The conflict escalated in September, when the Houthis seized the country's entire Red Sea coast, including the vital shipping lane of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, further disrupting global oil supplies.

Yemen's capital, Sanaa, which has been held by the Houthis for more than a decade, has come under sustained attack as government forces try to weaken the group's military capabilities.

Attacks on the Houthis have also spread across Yemen, including to the Saada region, the group's northern heartland.

On Sunday, Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address: "Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory."

But it is not yet clear whether this represents a new phase in the conflict.

The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government.

The Houthis are engaged in a fierce battle with government forces for control of the region, as they seek to secure coastal areas and, by extension, the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports.

Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz.

"They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP.

Away from Yemen, the Houthis are also trying to hurt the Saudis with an attack aimed at the country's economic lifeblood - oil.

On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east.

"Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites."

It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories".

But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis.

In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday.

On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west.

Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.

A war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of swathes of the country's north.

Riyadh intervened in the war the following year, leading an international coalition.

After several years of relative calm, the war reignited in July amid the widening conflict in the Middle East.

The Houthis have launched a blockade of Saudi energy exports, which have already been squeezed by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Woman's routine Uber ride takes alarming turn after her driver misses the exit
articles.summary: A viral TikTok video describes an Uber passenger's 3 a.m. ride turning alarming when her driver asked to stop at a parking garage to charge his EV. Experts weigh in.
articles.body: A late-night ride experience is raising questions about what passengers should do when a routine trip begins to feel uncomfortable. In a recent TikTok video, a woman said she was riding in an Uber at around 3 a.m. when her driver asked to stop at a parking garage for 15 to 20 minutes to charge his electric vehicle. The woman, according to her video, said the vehicle was at 43% charge — and that she was about 25 minutes from home at the time. FRIGHTENING OBJECT CAUGHT BY TSA INSIDE PASSENGER'S BASEBALL BAT-SHAPED FLASHLIGHT Her concern grew after the driver reportedly missed an exit, prompting her to question exactly where they were headed. "I don't want to get into a random parking lot with you," the woman can be heard telling the driver. "You also just missed the exit." Fox News Digital reached out to the woman who posted the TikTok video for additional details. The woman ultimately ended the trip and contacted police, according to the video. In a statement, Uber told Fox News Digital that it investigated the report and took action. SKYDIVERS WATCH PLANE VANISH FROM SIGHT, MAKE SPLIT-SECOND DECISION TO JUMP "Everyone deserves to feel safe and comfortable when using the Uber platform," an Uber spokesperson said. "We have investigated this report and taken appropriate action." The company pointed to safety features available through its app, including an emergency button, GPS tracking and the ability to share trip details with others. The incident has raised broader questions about what passengers can do if they feel uneasy during a rideshare trip. 'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS Dillon Abend, a recent college graduate and the founder and CEO of rideshare safety app 3rd-i, based in New Jersey, told Fox News Digital that an unexpected change in route can quickly raise concerns, particularly for someone traveling alone late at night. "Your heart just drops," he said. Abend said he's heard from hundreds of college students about situations that left them feeling uncomfortable during various rideshare trips. For passengers who begin feeling uncomfortable, seeking help can be challenging. "Almost everyone's reasoning in this situation is, 'I didn't want the driver three feet away to hear me call the police and have them act,'" Abend said. Technology can provide passengers with additional ways to stay connected or seek help during a ride-hailing trip, according to Abend. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Ideally, you want to share your location with people," he said. "Let a core group of three to five people know where you're going and the details of it." Before getting into a vehicle, check the license plate and confirm that the driver and vehicle match the information displayed in the rideshare app, he advised. New Jersey-based Seymour Josephson, co-president of the What's My Name Foundation, has been working with Uber and Lyft since July 2020 to promote rideshare safety on college campuses. He and his wife, Marci Josephson, established the foundation after their 21-year-old daughter, Samantha, was killed on March 29, 2019, when she mistakenly entered a vehicle she thought was the Uber she had hailed. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES The What's My Name Foundation encourages passengers to follow four steps before entering a ride-hailed vehicle: stop, ask, match and inform — known as the "SAMI" steps. People should stop before they enter the vehicle, ask the driver, "What's my name?" and match the vehicle's license plate with the information provided in the app. Fox News Digital reached out to Lyft for comment and details. "We want to make sure that we're not just getting into a car, but we're getting into the right car, the right Uber," Josephson said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Seymour Josephson said he is not looking to discourage people from using rideshare services, but to make the experience safer for everyone — both rider and driver. And it's securing that it is your ride by giving that pin to the driver before you get in."

articles.title: US Marine arrested over murder of woman in Okinawa, Japan
articles.summary: Japan's government lodged a formal protest with the US, demanding that military officials take action.
articles.body:
A US Marine has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a woman's body was found in a hotel in Okinawa, Japan, local officials say.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the crime as a "brutal and heinous" robbery and murder. She said she had urged the US to "enforce stricter discipline" of its personnel.

Japan's public broadcaster NHK identified the victim as Yagi Anna, 39, and the suspect as Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma.

"We are actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine," the Marine Corps said on social media, extending condolences to the victim's family.

Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the woman's body was discovered early Saturday morning in a hotel in Naha City, the capital of the Okinawa prefecture.

"Such an incident is utterly inexcusable and fills me with strong indignation," Koizumi wrote on social media, adding that "incidents and accidents involving U.S. military personnel cause significant anxiety to the local community and must never occur".

The US Embassy in Tokyo said that it was fully cooperating with the Japanese government and local police. Japan's foreign ministry said it summoned US ambassador George Glass to discuss the incident on Sunday.

Okinawa is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.

Okinawa Governor Genta Koja says the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline.

"The fact that this kind of event has happened again leaves us no choice but to conclude that the US military's efforts in maintaining discipline, educating personnel, and other such measures are completely ineffective," he said.

articles.title: Texas landowners feared border barriers would cut off access to the Rio Grande; an October 2 court order now blocks construction in the Big Bend sector while the legal challenge continues
articles.summary: A federal judge's ruling blocks further construction of border barriers in Texas' Big Bend region as landowners and environmental groups raise concerns about access to the Rio Grande and landscape disruption.
articles.body: A federal judge has blocked further construction of border barriers in Texas’ Big Bend region after landowners and local groups warned that the planned infrastructure could cut off their access to the Rio Grande and permanently alter the landscape.US District Judge Kathleen Cardone on Friday granted an environmental group's request for a preliminary injunction, keeping a halt on “ground-disturbing activities” in place while a broader legal challenge to the border projects moves through court.At the end of Friday's hearing, Cardone asked those in the courtroom to remain calm as she read her order from the bench. She found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their constitutional claims challenging the construction.The lawsuit was filed in April by the Center for Biological Diversity on behalf of the Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a nonprofit seeking to preserve a historic church in Presidio County, and Danny William Miller, a Rio Grande river guide and landowner whose property in Redford could be affected by the planned wall.The plaintiffs argue that five contracted border wall projects in the region are unconstitutional on several grounds, including that they violate the separation of powers and deprive citizens of their land.Landowners warn of losing access to the riverFor residents living along the Texas-Mexico border, the dispute is not limited to where a barrier would be built. They say the infrastructure could change how they use their land and reach the Rio Grande.According to the Big Bend Sentinel, Texas-based news outlet, Miller, who works as a river guide, told the court that having a wall built across his property and losing access to the river would be like “a bullet to the head”.He also argued that the desert landscape, once altered by construction, could not simply be restored.His work as a river guide, he said, would become “a tour of the military industrial complex, rather than a tour of the wilderness.”Bill Guerra-Addington, a Hudspeth County resident, similarly warned that a border barrier would effectively destroy his ranch.“They’re taking the river away from us, and it’s devastating,” he testified.Zeynep Graves, an attorney with the Center for Biological Diversity, argued that the consequences of the construction would extend beyond environmental damage.“The harm reaches far beyond the landscape itself,” Graves said in closing arguments.The lawsuit documents what the plaintiffs say could be lost if border barrier construction continues along the Rio Grande.Government says barriers are needed for border controlThe federal government has defended the need for physical border infrastructure, including in remote areas such as Big Bend.Officials argue that barriers are necessary to achieve what they describe as “operational control” of the border, meaning zero unauthorised border crossings.Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem made the case in a series of waivers that eased contracting requirements across the southwestern border.“Since the President took office, DHS has delivered the most secure border in history,” Noem wrote. “More can be done, however.”The government has also raised the possibility that changes in migrant routes could increase pressure on the Big Bend region if barriers are expanded elsewhere along the southern border.CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott has said the agency's goal includes protecting Big Bend National Park from potential future cartel activity.Why Big Bend has become a flashpointThe Big Bend sector stretches across a large portion of the Texas-Mexico border and includes both Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park.The region accounts for about a quarter of the length of the US-Mexico border but has historically recorded only between 1% and 3% of migrant apprehensions by US Customs and Border Protection each year.That contrast has become central to opposition against the planned infrastructure.News of the government's plans for barriers in Big Bend emerged in January 2026. Since then, opposition has grown across the region, bringing together residents from both sides of the political spectrum.The dispute has also pushed the government to modify aspects of its plans for physical border infrastructure, which includes walls, roads, fences, lighting and sensors.The projects involved in the wider programme represent more than $7.5 billion in government contracts.Despite the opposition, construction activity has continued in parts of the region. Contractors have bulldozed new roads in Big Bend National Park after the government waived the Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act to facilitate what it described as the “expeditious construction of barriers and roads” along the border.Six lawsuits challenge Big Bend wall plansFriday's ruling is the latest development in a growing legal fight over the border infrastructure.Six lawsuits have now been filed over the planned Big Bend wall.Earlier this week, a judge rejected a request for a temporary restraining order in a separate case seeking to stop work in and around Big Bend National Park. articles.summary: Cusat researchers secured an Indian patent for compact microstrip patch antenna technology to reduce radiation exposure and SAR in wireless and body-centric devices.
articles.body: Kochi: Researchers at Cochin University of Science and Technology (Cusat) have received an Indian patent for a compact microstrip patch antenna technology designed to reduce radiation directed towards the human body from wireless devices.The technology is aimed at reducing the absorption of electromagnetic energy by the human body while maintaining a compact antenna design.
